extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical Euclidean geometry (Book VI)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of theorems, corollaries, constructions and definitions from Euclid's Elements Book VI (propositions XIX–XXXIII in this chunk), focused on similar figures, parallelograms, and related constructions. Useful for learners or implementers who need the explicit geometric principles and construction constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar triangles — area ratio (Prop. XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar triangles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their homologous sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If triangles ABC and DEF are similar with corresponding sides BC and EF, then the ratio of the areas (or of the triangles) ABC:DEF is the square (duplicate ratio) of BC:EF. Euclid proves by inserting a third proportional and showing corresponding triangles are equal, then invoking the property that if three lines are proportionals the first to the third is the duplicate ratio of the first to the second.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — triangle-on-line proportionality (cor. to XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three straight lines are proportionals, as the first is to the third, so is any triangle upon the first to a similar and similarly described triangle upon the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the duplicate-ratio property of similar triangles, Euclid deduces that proportionality of straight lines transfers to proportionality of similarly described triangles on those lines: given a:b = c:d = e:f etc., triangles on a and c are to each other as triangles on b and d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar polygons divide into similar triangles; area ratio (Prop. XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar polygons may be divided into the same number of similar triangles, each to each having the same ratio as the polygons; the polygons have to one another the duplicate ratio of that which their homologous sides have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given two similar polygons (ABCDE and FGHKL), join diagonals to divide both into corresponding triangles (ABE~FGL, EBC~LGH, etc.). Each pair of corresponding triangles is similar and has the same ratio as the polygons; hence the ratio of the polygons equals the duplicate ratio of a homologous side (e.g., AB:FG squared equals polygon ABCDE:FGHKL). The proof proceeds by comparing corresponding triangles pairwise and adding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — universal duplicate-ratio for rectilineal figures (cor.1 to XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar rectilineal figures (of any number of sides) are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their homologous sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid extends the triangle/polygon result to any rectilineal figure by partitioning into triangles or reducing to already proved triangle cases: area ratios of any similar rectilineal figures equal the square of the ratio of homologous sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary — use of third proportional for figures (cor.2 to XX)
rubrics_metrics.description: If to two homologous sides AB and FG a third proportional M is taken, then AB:M is the duplicate ratio of AB:FG, and correspondingly any rectilineal figure on AB has to the similar figure on FG that duplicate ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid uses the construction of a third proportional to show how to translate the duplicate-ratio relation via three proportionals: if AB:FG = FG: M, then the figure on AB is to the figure on FG as AB:M (i.e., duplicate ratio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity of similarity for rectilineal figures (Prop. XXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectilineal figures which are similar to the same rectilineal figure are also similar to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A~C and B~C (each equiangular with proportional sides about equal angles), then A and B are equiangular and have proportional sides about equal angles; hence A~B. This establishes similarity is an equivalence relation (transitive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of figures built on proportional lines (Prop. XXII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four straight lines are proportionals, the similar rectilineal figures similarly described upon them are proportionals; conversely, if the figures are proportionals, the straight lines are proportionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given AB:CD = EF:GH and similar figures KAB, LCD on AB,CD and MF, NH on EF,GH, then KAB:LCD = MF:NH. Proof uses taking third proportionals to reduce to earlier results. Conversely, if figures are in proportion then the underlying generating lines are in proportion (construction reduces to equal-diameter argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound ratio for equiangular parallelograms (Prop. XXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equiangular parallelograms have to one another the ratio which is compounded of the ratios of their sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two parallelograms are equiangular (corresponding sides proportional), the ratio of the parallelograms equals the product (compound) of the ratios of corresponding sides (e.g., ratio of base1:base2 compounded with side1:side2). Euclid proves by reducing to proportions between constructed segments and using properties of parallelograms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelograms about a diagonal are similar to whole and to each other (Prop. XXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelograms constructed about the diameter (diagonal) of any parallelogram are similar to the whole parallelogram and to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a parallelogram ABCD with diagonal AC, the parallelograms constructed on AC (about that diameter) are equiangular and have corresponding sides proportional to the whole; therefore each small parallelogram is similar to ABCD and to the others. Proof uses parallel lines and equal opposite sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: describe figure similar to one and equal to another (Prop. XXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a rectilineal figure ABC (to be similar to) and a rectilineal D (to be equal to), construct a rectilineal figure similar to ABC and equal to D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's construction: describe a parallelogram equal to ABC on a straight line BC, another parallelogram equal to D on CE, make mean proportional between BC and CF, describe on that mean a figure similar to ABC; use proportionality of applied figures to produce a figure KGH similar to ABC and equal to D. The proposition gives a step-by-step construction and checks equality via subtracting common parts and proportional arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-diameter criterion for similar parallelograms (Prop. XXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two similar parallelograms have a common angle and are similarly situated, they are about the same diameter (share the same diagonal line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two similar, similarly situated parallelograms share angle DAB, then assuming otherwise leads to a contradiction via constructing a parallelogram sharing the other diameter; proportionality of sides forces equality of segments implying impossibility, hence they must be about the same diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: 'applied', 'deficient', 'exceeding' parallelogram
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions used in following propositions: applying a parallelogram to a straight line means it has that line as a side; 'applied deficient by a parallelogram' means the applied parallelogram's base is less than the full line and so is deficient by a parallelogram; 'applied exceeding by a parallelogram' means its base is greater and it exceeds by a parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit definitional conventions used in subsequent constructions and comparisons (Props. XXVII–XXIX). They determine how applied parallelograms relate to a given straight line and the notion of 'defect' or 'excess' as a specific parallelogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximization among applied, deficient parallelograms (Prop. XXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all parallelograms applied to the same straight line and deficient by parallelograms similar and similarly situated to a given one, the parallelogram applied to the half and similar to its defect is the greatest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given AB divided at midpoint C, the parallelogram applied to AC and deficient by a parallelogram similar to the given defect is larger than any parallelogram applied to any other part of AB and deficient by a similar defect. Proof examines cases AK>AC and AK<AC, constructs diameters and compares sums/differences to show AD > AF for any other AF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction constraint for applying parallelogram deficient by similar defect (Prop. XXVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply to a given straight line a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure and deficient by a parallelogram similar to a given parallelogram, the given rectilineal figure must not be greater than the parallelogram applied to the half of the line whose defect is similar to the given parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid provides a construction: divide AB in half, apply a parallelogram on half similar to defect, if the completed parallelogram equals the desired figure stop; otherwise adjust by subtracting or adding a similar parallelogram (KM) to reach equality. The initial size constraint (not greater than parallelogram on half) is necessary for constructibility without further modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: apply parallelogram exceeding by similar parallelogram (Prop. XXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: To a given straight line apply a parallelogram equal to a given figure, exceeding by a parallelogram similar to another given parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's method: divide AB in half, construct a parallelogram on half similar to the given defect, construct a larger parallelogram equal to that and the target figure together and then form a gnomon whose remainder equals the target figure; complete with diameters to obtain the parallelogram applied to AB exceeding by a parallelogram similar to the given one. The proof checks equality and similarity of the excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: cut line in extreme and mean ratio (Prop. XXX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a straight line AB, to cut it in extreme and mean ratio (i.e., find point E so that AB:AE = AE:EB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid gives a construction via describing on AB a square and applying to AC a parallelogram equal to that square and exceeding by a figure similar to the square, deducing AE satisfies the extreme and mean ratio. An alternative method: choose C on AB so rectangle AB·BC equals square on AC; then as BA:AC = AC:CB and AB is cut in extreme and mean ratio at C. Both constructive methods are provided and proven by proportional arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean generalization — similar figures on sides of right triangle (Prop. XXXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: In right-angled triangles, the rectilineal figure described upon the side opposite the right angle is equal to the similar and similarly described figures upon the sides containing the right angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes Pythagoras: for any figures (not just squares) similarly and similarly described on the three sides of a right triangle, the figure on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the figures on the legs. Proof uses the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse, similarity of the smaller triangles to the whole, and the property that if three straight lines are proportionals then the corresponding figures follow the same proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collinearity from proportional sides with parallels (Prop. XXXII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles have two sides of one proportional to two sides of the other and are joined at one angle so their homologous sides are parallel, then the remaining sides are in a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given triangles ABC and DCE with BA:AC = CD:DE and AB∥DC, AC∥DE, Euclid shows by angle equalities and proportionality that the sum of certain angles equals two right angles, hence the external sides BC and CE are collinear. Proof uses angle equalities from parallel lines and equiangularity from proportional sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angles and sectors in equal circles are proportional to circumferences (Prop. XXXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles, angles (at centres or circumferences) and sectors are to one another in the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given equal circles ABC and DEF, the angle at center BGC corresponds to EHF. Euclid uses equimultiples of circumferences and the additivity of equal arc multiples to show: circumference BC : EF = angle BGC : EHF, and hence the inscribed angles are similarly proportional (angles at centre double inscribed angles). He also shows corresponding sectors are proportional to their arcs by dissecting arcs into equal pieces and comparing corresponding triangular segments.
